STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Portobello mushroom’s benefits for human and pet health can be attributed to the abundance of components like polysaccharides, which may have antioxidant effects by working as adaptogens and immunomodulators
  • Glutathione, which is found in all mushrooms, is called the “master antioxidant;” it has many functions in humans and companion animals, such as supporting liver function, boosting immunity, repairing tissues and protecting mitochondrial function

  • Another nutrient in portobello mushrooms, conjugated linoleic acid (CLA), has “anticarcinogenic, antiobese, antidiabetic and antihypertensive properties”
  • Opt for spray-free organic portobello mushrooms, whenever possible, to ensure they’re truly sustainable and free of harmful chemicals

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published February 15, 2023.

Edible medicinal and culinary mushrooms have many benefits for your pet’s health, which is why this type of food is one of the best to share with your dogs and cats. Just remember this rule: Only feed your pets mushrooms that you would eat yourself. All mushrooms sold at the grocery store or market that are intended for human consumption are also safe for pets.

One of the most popular mushroom varieties in the culinary world is portobello, and it is enjoyed by humans in many ways. Continue reading to find out what benefits this versatile superfood can offer your pet.

What Are Portobello Mushrooms?

Also called portobella or portabella mushrooms, Agaricus bisporus is a large, dark-brown, meaty type of mushroom that’s known for its dense, chewy texture and rich, savory taste.1 Each mushroom measures between 4 and 6 inches in diameter, making it the largest type of cultivated mushroom.2 Its flavor is described as “umami” — rich, earthy and meaty — thanks to an amino acid, called glutamate, found in the mushroom.3

Because of widespread misinformation on the internet stating “all mushrooms are poisonous for pets,” many pet owners have ended up denying their pets the amazing healing properties of medicinal mushrooms. But don't let these myths scare you away from giving your pet these foods. Mushrooms like portobello are perfectly safe for your pets. They offer your pets protein, nutrients like B vitamins, copper, selenium and phosphorus,4 and various antioxidants.

Cremini, White Button, and Portobello — Same Mushroom, Different Names


Did you know that these three mushrooms are actually one kind, just varying in maturity? The white button mushroom is the youngest variety, while the portobello is the most mature of the three. Cremini is in between — in some instances, it’s called “baby bella” or “baby portobello.”5


Portobello has a more intense flavor than the other two because as mushrooms grow and mature, they lose their water content, leaving you with a more concentrated flavor.6

CLA in Portobellos May Have Anticancer Properties

Mushrooms like portobello are dense in nutrients because, as fungi, they scavenge organic matter — they absorb the nutrients from the ground and from decaying wood, and even manure. The nutrients have various benefits to human and animal health, such as eliminating toxins from the body and scavenging disease-causing free radicals.

One of the nutrients in portobello mushrooms is conjugated linoleic acid (CLA),7 which has “anticarcinogenic, antiobese, antidiabetic and antihypertensive properties.”8 A 2008 animal study supports the notion that this fatty acid may be beneficial for cancer prevention, as it was found to help inhibit prostate tumor growth in mice subjects. According to the study authors:9

“The data provided by this study illustrate the anticancer potential of phytochemicals in mushroom extract both in vitro and in vivo and supports the recommendation of white button mushroom as a dietary component that may aid in the prevention of prostate cancer in men.”

In companion animals, CLA may also help manage weight, which may be especially helpful for obese or overweight pets. Rodent studies found that CLA helped enhance fatty acid oxidation, leading to as much as 60% lower body fat and 14% increased lean body mass.10

Bioactive Polysaccharides in Portobellos Help Boost Immunity

Portobello mushroom’s benefits for human and pet health can be attributed to the abundance of components like polysaccharides, which have antioxidant effects and work as adaptogens and immunomodulators. They also exert antitumor effects by stimulating apoptosis (cancer cell death).11 A 2022 study also noted:12

“Mushroom polysaccharides prevent oncogenesis, show direct antitumor activity against various allogeneic and syngeneic tumors, and prevent tumor metastasis. Polysaccharides from mushrooms do not attack cancer cells directly, but produce their antitumor effects by activating different immune responses in the host.”

The primary class of polysaccharides found in mushrooms are beta-glucans, which have “anticancer, immunomodulating, anticholesterolemic, antioxidant, and neuroprotective activities.”13 They work by binding to a membrane receptor and inducing these biological responses.

A 2020 study found that beta-glucans may help improve dogs’ immunity. When blood-enriched monocytes were stimulated with beta-glucans, the researchers noted increased production of pro-inflammatory and antimicrobial compounds as a response to bacterial stimuli.14 Another way that beta-glucans may play a role in immunity is via gut health. Beta-glucans may have a prebiotic effect,15 helping to feed the good bacteria in your pet’s system.

Glutathione — The Master Antioxidant in Portobello Mushrooms

Glutathione, which is found in all mushrooms, is called the “master antioxidant,” and for good reason. It has a number of functions, such as breaking down free radicals, supporting immune function and assisting apoptosis and even DNA production.16

Just as in humans, glutathione has many functions in pet health, such as supporting the liver, boosting the immune system, repairing tissues and protecting mitochondrial function.17 One 2009 study, for example, noted that ill dogs had depleted glutathione levels compared to healthy dogs, supporting the notion that having less-than-optimal levels of this antioxidant can affect illness severity and increase risk of mortality. The researchers noted:18

“In summary, GSH [erythrocyte glutathione] concentrations were significantly lower in ill compared with healthy dogs, and GSH depletion was correlated with both illness severity and increased mortality. These results suggest that GSH concentrations may be a marker of illness severity, and may be prognostic of clinical outcome in ill dogs.”

The mushroom variety that contains the highest amount of glutathione is porcini, but that doesn’t mean portobellos don’t have a lot to offer as well. In fact, these mushrooms have higher amounts of glutathione than most foods.19

Ergothioneine — The Longevity Vitamin

An antioxidant that goes hand-in-hand with glutathione,20 ergothioneine has been dubbed the “longevity vitamin” due to its potential to help inhibit chronic diseases associated with aging.21 This potent dietary antioxidant amino acid functions as an anti-inflammatory agent and may help mitigate chronic neurodegenerative illnesses. A 2020 study noted:22

“Decreased blood and/or plasma levels of ergothioneine have been observed in some diseases, suggesting that a deficiency could be relevant to the disease onset or progression.”

Ergothioneine’s beneficial effects for pets stem from its ability to help manage oxidative stress in mitochondria. It may also help protect heart and brain function.23 Ergothioneine accumulates intercellularly, inside the mitochondria and nuclei to provide protection against oxidative damage in DNA.24 In animal studies, ergothioneine had a protective effect on the liver and intestines.25,26

Top Portobello Mushroom Producers in the US

Portobello mushrooms are the most popular variety cultivated in the U.S., accounting for approximately 90% of mushroom production in the country.27

There are 33 U.S. states that grow mushrooms,28 and Pennsylvania — particularly southeastern Pennsylvania, near the town of Kennett Square29 — accounts for half of the production. California and Florida rank second and third place, respectively.30

Biologically Active Amines Promote Longevity

Another reason why mushrooms like portobello are so good for your pets is because they contain polyamines, which are valued for their longevity advantage. Polyamines, which work by binding with negatively charged molecules, like DNA, RNA and proteins, can have effects on cell growth, survival and proliferation. When there are changes to polyamine levels in your body, it can affect the aging and disease processes.31

The most potent type of polyamines in mushrooms is spermidine, which, according to one study, may have molecular and physiological effects. According to the authors:32

“Consistently, extra supply of spermidine prolongs the life span across species in an autophagy-dependent manner and counteracts age-associated pathologies such as cardiovascular disease, neurodegeneration, and cancer.”

Did You Know?

Portobello mushroom’s scientific name comes from the Greek word “agrarius,” which means “growing in the fields.” Meanwhile, its name comes from a town in Italy, where it originated.33

Are Portobello Mushrooms Sustainable?

Mushrooms like portobello are among the most environmentally friendly and sustainable crops, mainly because their farmers are able to convert waste and byproducts from other agriculture sectors, which they then use as compost. This is why mushroom growers are dubbed the “ultimate recyclers.”

Through smart management and efficient production practices, mushrooms also have a very small carbon footprint. Every pound of mushrooms requires only around 2 gallons of water and 1.0 kilowatt of electricity. Further, according to the American Mushroom Institute:34

“[I]f you added up all the emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2, a greenhouse gas) from producing that one pound of button mushrooms — from the compost recipe all the way through to what you purchase in the store — it is the equivalent of just 0.7 pounds of CO2. To give some perspective of how small a carbon footprint that is, using one gallon of fuel in the U.S. emits nearly 20 pounds of CO2.”

How to Safely Give Portobello Mushrooms to Your Pets

“Whatever the mushroom variety, make sure to always steer clear of mushrooms growing in the wild.”

Unless you are an expert wild forager of mushrooms, only feed those that come from reputable growers and farmers markets. Opt for spray-free organic mushrooms, whenever possible, to ensure that they’re truly sustainable and free of harmful chemicals.

Wash portobello mushrooms under cold running water quickly before preparing them. Research suggests the nutritional properties of mushrooms, including beta-glucans, are more accessible if mushrooms are gently cooked prior to serving.35 Steaming or sautéing them quickly in coconut oil is suggested. Since portobellos are a bit large, make sure to chop or slice them before sharing with your pet.

When using as treats or toppers, serve the mushrooms plain, without any seasonings. They can make for a wholesome training treat or a tasty meal topper to your pet’s nutritionally balanced, species-appropriate homemade diet. You can puree them and spread on lick mats, slice and stuff in an interactive toy, or use them as an ingredient in homemade training treats or homemade meals.

item.title: Without This, Pets' Skin and Coat Can Suffer
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • If your pet’s coat and skin get dry and flaky during the winter months, it’s probably time to take a proactive approach to year-round maintenance
  • A very important step in improving the health of the skin and coat is ensuring your dog or cat’s diet is rich in omega-3 essential fatty acids
  • It’s also important to rule out underlying medical conditions known to contribute to poor coat and skin condition
  • Regular coat brushing, including for kitties who need a little help with their grooming, will go a long way to remove dead skin and hair; bathing your pet as often as needed will also help keep her skin and coat in good condition
  • Topical coconut oil treatments, applied after a bath, can help strengthen the skin's lipid barrier and improve resistance to yeast and opportunistic bacteria

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published December 30, 2017.

Winter is here in most parts of the U.S., and just as cold temperatures and indoor heating tend to make your own hair and skin feel dry and flaky, the same thing can happen to furry family members. But keeping your dog's or cat's coat in healthy condition year-round, including this time of year, is probably easier than you think. More often than not, a pet's flaky skin and dry coat are due to one or more factors, including:

  • Dietary deficiencies
  • An underlying medical condition
  • Lack of regular grooming
  • Infrequent baths (or in rare cases, too frequent baths)

If your dog's or kitty's coat is in bad shape due to one or more of these causes, winter's cold temperatures and low humidity will exacerbate the problem. Your goal should be to consistently maintain your pet's skin and coat in optimum condition year-round to help avoid seasonal problems.

Ensuring Your Pet's Diet Is Rich in Omega-3 Essential Fatty Acids

Lack of omega-3 fatty acids in the diet is a common cause of excessively flaky skin in pets. Dogs and cats need an abundance of omega-3s to be healthy from the inside out. If you live in a dry climate, your pet may need fewer baths than dogs or cats living in areas with higher humidity. As a general rule, the more humid the climate, the more skin irritation is seen in pets, and the more often they need to be bathed.

Select a gentle, organic shampoo specifically designed for dogs or cats, and avoid oatmeal shampoos. Oatmeal may be a soothing ingredient, but grain-based shampoos are not a good idea for most dogs and cats. In fact, the only pets that truly benefit from oatmeal shampoos are those with poison oak or poison ivy reactions.

You might also want to follow up with an all-natural, species-specific conditioner to moisturize and condition your pet's skin and coat, or a homemade healing rinse.

Another Option to Improve Dry, Flaky Skin: Coconut Oil Skin Treatments

Topical coconut oil treatments can be very helpful in improving the integrity of flaking skin. They also support the lipid barrier, which makes your pet's skin healthier and more resistant to pathogens like yeast and opportunistic bacteria.

This treatment can be used with both short and long-haired dogs, but it will obviously be more challenging with a long-haired pet. It's important to do coconut oil treatments on clean skin, so bathe your pet first and dry her thoroughly. Using 100% organic, cold-pressed, orangutan-friendly human-grade coconut oil is recommended.

Coconut oil contains lauric acid, which supports the immune system whether taken orally or used topically. item.title: Does Your Pet Panic During Storms?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • An estimated 25% to 50% of dogs experience noise anxiety, and thunderstorms are among the most common triggers. Storm phobia can worsen over time if it is left unaddressed
  • Storms frighten dogs for more than the noise alone; sensitivity to shifting air pressure and even static building up in a dog's coat can all play a part
  • Watch for obvious signs of anxiety, such as pacing, panting, trembling, or drooling, as well as subtler cues like lip-licking, yawning, tucked tail, and pinned-back ears
  • Giving your dog a safe den-like space, blocking out lightning and thunder, offering a calming activity, providing reassurance, and behavior modification training can help them get through a storm
  • A sudden new fear of storms in a dog that was never bothered before should be discussed with a veterinarian, as it can signal pain, heart disease, or a neurological problem

Why do thunderstorms send so many dogs into a panic? The loud thunder is only part of the reason. If your dog trembles and hides every time a storm rolls in, what you are seeing is a genuine fear response rather than an overreaction.

Storm phobia is recognized as a behavioral disorder that combines physical, emotional, and behavioral reactions.1 Understanding what is driving it can help you respond better as a pet parent.

Why Thunder Turns Your Dog Into a Nervous Wreck

An estimated 25% to 50% of all dogs experience some form of noise anxiety,2 and thunder is a common trigger. In an article published by the American Kennel Club (AKC), certified trainer Trista Miller explains that dogs hear thunder well before we do.

Their hearing is far more sensitive than ours, and fear of loud noise is baked into them as a survival instinct.3 Dogs may also detect changes in air pressure, allowing them to sense an approaching storm before the first drop of rain hits your window.

There is another factor you might not expect: static electricity. A feature in Vets of the Rockies cited that thunderstorms charge the surrounding air, and that electrical charge can build up in your dog's coat, especially if they are a larger breed or have a thick double coat.4 When their nose touches metal, like a doorknob or a food bowl, they may feel a small shock.

This invisible discomfort may explain why your dog beelines for the bathroom or basement during a storm. Plumbing and porcelain fixtures may help dissipate static electricity, making a bathtub or tiled room feel safer than other areas of the house.5 Without proper support, storm anxiety tends to get worse with every passing storm season and can take a toll on both your dog's health and quality of life.6

Early Signs Your Dog Is Anxious

Dogs often show subtle signs of anxiety before more obvious behaviors start, such as pacing, trembling, or drooling. University of Florida College of Veterinary Medicine clinical behaviorist Terry Curtis notes that early stress signals may include:7

  • Yawning — A big, sudden yawn that has nothing to do with being tired is one of the clearest early signs that your dog is feeling uneasy or overwhelmed, particularly when it occurs alongside other changes in body language, and it is easy to miss if you are not looking.
  • Frequent lip-licking and widened eyes — Repeatedly licking their lips paired with wide, alert eyes may indicate that your dog has noticed something unsettling in their environment.
  • Pinned-back ears and a tucked tail — Ears held flat against the head and a tucked or lowered tail often signal fear, nervousness, or an attempt to make the body appear smaller.

Catching these cues early gives you a chance to step in before your dog's anxiety escalates. If you notice them before the storm arrives, guide your dog to a quiet, familiar space where they can feel more secure.

It Is Not Always Storm Anxiety

If your dog suddenly becomes fearful during thunderstorms, even though it never seemed to bother them before, do not assume it is simply a new fear they have developed.8 A new sensitivity to storms may sometimes be linked to pain, heart problems, and neurological conditions. If your dog's reaction to storms seems to come out of nowhere, it is a good idea to talk with your veterinarian to rule out any underlying health issues.

Storm anxiety also rarely exists as a sole anxiety. Dogs with storm phobias often have other noise sensitivities and frequently also have separation anxiety.9,10 Also, scientists have found a link between level of exercise dogs receives daily and both noise and separation anxiety behaviors.11 Dogs receiving more daily exercise exhibited less anxiety behaviors. If your pet is dealing with storm phobias, talk to your veterinarian about your pet’s sensitivities and behavior, and see if adjusting your pet’s exercise program could be helpful.

Storm anxiety does not just affect your dog's emotions. Repeated episodes of fear and stress can increase their heart rate, raise stress hormones, disrupt digestion, and even put them at risk of injury.12 Some dogs become so distressed during storms that they damage their teeth or injure themselves while trying to escape.

Storms can occasionally pose a direct physical danger as well. Although lightning strikes are rare, they require immediate emergency care. If your dog has been struck, take them to an emergency veterinarian immediately, even if they seem normal at first, because serious internal injuries may not be immediately visible.13

Help Your Pet Feel Safe During a Storm

The good news is that storm anxiety is manageable, even when it does not disappear completely. For many dogs, a combination of calming strategies and small changes to their environment usually beats any single fix on its own.

  • Create a comfortable, safe space — Dogs tend to gravitate toward den-like spots, such as a crate, closet, or bathroom, because enclosed spaces feel safer. Make the space comfortable and cozy with a soft bed, familiar blankets, and their favorite toys. Let your dog choose whether to stay there rather than forcing them inside.14 And as we talked about above, if your dog feels safest in the bathroom, give them access. Being near plumbing is very grounding for them.
  • Muffle storm sounds and flashes — Close your curtains or blinds to block out flashes of lightning, turn on indoor lights, and use a TV, radio, fan, or white noise machine to reduce the sound of thunder.15 The AKC adds that classical music tends to have a soothing effect on dogs.16,17
  • Keep their mouth busy — Chewing and licking are naturally calming activities for many dogs, so a lick mat smeared with peanut butter, a stuffed food toy, or a puzzle feeder can help keep them occupied and redirect nervous energy.18 Make sure any peanut butter you use is free of xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.
  • Try an anxiety vest — Anxiety vests work by applying gentle, steady pressure around the body, which may help some dogs feel more secure. Introduce the vest well before a storm arrives so your dog has time to get used to wearing it.19
  • Tire them out ahead of time — If a storm is in the forecast, try fitting in a brisk walk or active play session beforehand. A dog who has burned off excess energy may settle more easily once the weather turns.20
  • Let your dog curl up to you — It is a common myth that comforting your dog during a storm reinforces their fear. Fear is an involuntary physical response, not a behavior your affection can accidentally encourage.21 It is okay to let them stay close, speak to them calmly, or gently pet them if that seems to help. Follow their lead, as some dogs prefer physical reassurance while others want space.

If your dog continues to tremble, hide, panic, or try to escape despite these measures, talk to your veterinarian. They can discuss additional treatment options and recommend behavior-modification techniques that gradually help your dog form calmer associations with storms.22

You cannot stop the rain and thunder from coming, but you can help your dog get through it. The better you understand your dog's triggers and needs, the better prepared you will be to help them feel safe when the next storm arrives.

  • 2 Veterinary Clinics of North America: Small Animal Practice Volume 38, Issue 5, September 2008, Pages 1081-1106
  • 3 American Kennel Club, September 30, 2025

item.title: 5 Subtle Signs Your Dog Dislikes Children
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Some dogs are uncomfortable around children, and the cause can include a bad experience in the past, “kids being kids” behavior that can feel threatening and/or lack of socialization to youngsters during puppyhood

  • Whining

  • International Association of Animal Behavior Consultants (I.A.A.B.C.)
  • Karen Pryor Academy
  • Academy for Dog Trainers
  • Pet Professional Guild
  • Fear Free Pets

Our aim is for school children to learn to handle dogs safely, to develop their own sense of responsibility, along with knowledge and understanding of the biology, behaviour and 'language' of dogs.
This resource will help school children see how they can modify their behaviour around dogs so they can interact safely and happily. Understanding a dog's needs and instinctive behaviours is essential in developing a safe and rewarding relationship.”1

  • The wolf pack
  • The dog's family
  • The dog's human family
  • How to behave when you meet a strange dog
  • Caring for your dog

item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Boswellia serrata, also known as Indian frankincense, is a tree resin used for centuries in Ayurvedic medicine and is now backed by modern veterinary research for its ability to support joint health in dogs with osteoarthritis
  • Its active compounds — boswellic acids, especially AKBA — work through a different anti-inflammatory pathway than NSAIDs, targeting the 5-LOX enzyme rather than cyclooxygenase, and also help protect cartilage by slowing enzymes that degrade collagen
  • A landmark Swiss clinical trial found that 71% of dogs with chronic joint and spine disease showed improvement within two weeks of taking a standardized boswellia extract, with reductions in lameness, pain, and stiffness by the six-week mark
  • Boswellia's strongest evidence comes when it is combined with complementary ingredients like undenatured type II collagen (UC-II), curcumin, glucosamine, chondroitin, or omega-3s — the multi-front approach consistently outperforms boswellia used alone
  • Boswellia should not be given alongside blood thinners like aspirin, warfarin, or heparin, and should be avoided in pregnant or nursing dogs; always use a dog-specific product and consult your veterinarian before starting

Your dog used to bound off the couch. Now they pause, stretch, and take the long slow route down. They still love their walks, but they take a moment longer to get up in the morning. That first minute of stiffness after a long nap is starting to feel like a pattern rather than a one-off.

Aging joints are one of the most common reasons pet parents look for something gentler to help their dog. One of the plant compounds that keeps coming up in veterinary conversations is boswellia, a tree resin with an ancient history and a growing body of modern research behind it.

What Boswellia Actually Is

Boswellia, also known as Indian frankincense, is the resin extracted from the Boswellia serrata tree, native to India and the Middle East. For centuries, it has been part of traditional Ayurvedic medicine, prized for its anti-inflammatory and anti-rheumatic properties.1

Modern veterinary science has started to catch up with what those traditions long claimed. Boswellia is now one of the most extensively studied natural compounds for supporting joint health in dogs, and it shows up regularly in veterinary joint supplements.2,3

Traditional healers in India used the aromatic resin for everything from swelling to breathing issues. Contemporary researchers are exploring the effects of Boswellia not only in osteoarthritis and joint disease, but also cancer, viral infections, gut inflammation, and even anxiety behaviors.4 Osteoarthritis research has found that boswellia does do a specific job well: it helps to quiet the kind of chronic inflammation that shows up in arthritic joints.

How It Works

The active ingredients in boswellia are boswellic acids. Six different forms of these compounds have been identified in the resin, but one in particular does most of the heavy lifting: acetyl-11-keto-beta-boswellic acid (AKBA). AKBA works differently from the anti-inflammatory drugs most pet parents are familiar with.

Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) target one specific enzyme pathway (cyclooxygenase). However, boswellic acids target a different pathway, an enzyme called 5-lipoxygenase, or 5-LOX, which is involved in producing leukotrienes. Leukotrienes are powerful inflammatory chemicals that can degrade joint tissue over time.

Because boswellia hits a different inflammatory pathway, it can complement conventional treatments rather than duplicating them. It also appears to have chondroprotective effects, meaning it helps protect joint cartilage by slowing the enzymes that break down collagen and other structural tissues.5

That combination — dialing down inflammation while also helping preserve the cushion inside the joint — is what makes boswellia genuinely interesting to veterinarians who work with arthritic dogs. It is not just a pain reliever; it is a tissue supporter as well.

What Canine Research Shows

A landmark Swiss veterinary trial gave 29 dogs with joint and spine disease a standardized boswellia extract at 400 milligrams (mg) per 10 kilograms (kg) of body weight daily for six weeks. Within just two weeks, 71% of the dogs showed overall improvement.6

By the end of the six-week trial, researchers noted meaningful reductions in lameness, localized pain, and stiffness. Since then, boswellia has been studied more often as part of multi-ingredient joint formulas. Here are other notable findings:7

  • A 2022 trial tested a supplement combining boswellia with chlorophyll, green tea extract, glucosamine, chondroitin sulfate, hyaluronic acid, and type II collagen in dogs with osteoarthritis. The supplemented dogs showed less pain and fewer arthritis signs.8
  • A 2023 study found that dogs with osteoarthritis receiving cannabis sativa oil, boswellia phytosome, and ginger had less pain, inflammation, and oxidative stress.9
  • A 2024 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial, researchers found that undenatured type II collagen combined with boswellia showed improved mobility in dogs with osteoarthritis.10
  • A 2023 scoping review published in the journal Animals concluded that boswellia, especially when paired with other evidence-based ingredients, produces meaningful benefits for dogs dealing with osteoarthritis.11

The honest caveat: many of these studies used multi-ingredient supplements, which means the improvements cannot be pinned entirely on boswellia alone. What the research suggests is that boswellia works well as part of a thoughtful, well-designed joint support formula.

Synergistic Combinations

Some of the most compelling recent research looks at how boswellia performs alongside other joint-supporting ingredients. In the 2024 study mentioned above, for example, a supplement containing undenatured type II collagen (UC-II) and boswellia improved mobility in dogs with mild-to-moderate osteoarthritis within just four weeks, based on owner evaluations.12

The combination of boswellia and curcumin (the active compound in turmeric) has also received attention. Studies have found that pairing these two significantly improved joint function and reduced discomfort. Researchers point to their complementary anti-inflammatory mechanisms as the likely reason.13

This is worth knowing when you are shopping. A joint supplement that combines boswellia with ingredients like UC-II collagen, glucosamine, chondroitin, curcumin, or omega-3 fatty acids is more likely to deliver noticeable results than boswellia used entirely on its own.

The takeaway is not that boswellia alone is weak. It is that joint pain in dogs is usually a multi-faceted problem, and formulations that address several angles at once, and use synergistic ingredients, tend to outperform any single ingredient in isolation.

Safety and Side Effects

Boswellia has a generally favorable safety profile in dogs. The Swiss clinical trial reported only brief, reversible digestive changes in a small number of dogs, and only one of those was linked to the supplement itself. Long-term safety studies have found that properly standardized boswellia extracts are well tolerated at recommended doses.14 That said, side effects are possible. Reported ones include:

  • Mild gastrointestinal upset (vomiting, diarrhea, or gas)
  • A slight decrease in blood clotting times
  • Occasional allergic reactions, which can develop even after weeks of use

Because sensitivities can develop over time with repeated exposure, it is worth watching your dog for any changes throughout the course of treatment, not just at the start.

Interactions Worth Knowing About

Just because something is natural does not mean it plays nicely with every other medication. Boswellia should not be given alongside drugs that affect blood clotting or platelet function, including aspirin, heparin, warfarin, and other blood thinners.

It should also be used with caution, or avoided entirely, in pregnant or nursing dogs, since safe use has not been established in those situations. Always share a full list of your dog's medications and supplements with your veterinarian before starting anything new.15,16

How to Give It

Boswellia comes in several forms: powders, capsules, and tablets. It can be given with or without food, ideally at the same time each day. Remember these practical guidelines:17,18,19

  • Use a dog-specific product — Human boswellia supplements may contain ingredients, combinations, or dosages that are not appropriate for dogs. When possible, choose a supplement made specifically for pets.
  • Look for standardization — Products standardized for AKBA content tend to deliver more consistent results. Advanced extracts with improved bioavailability can achieve stronger effects at lower doses.
  • Check for quality markers — Supplements produced in National Animal Supplement Council (NASC) certified facilities that follow Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) generally offer better assurance of ingredient purity and label accuracy.
  • Be patient with the timeline — Most dogs show improvement within two to four weeks of consistent use, though some may take up to eight weeks to show significant changes. This is a supplement that rewards patience, not one that produces overnight results.
  • And loop in your veterinarian — Boswellia is not a replacement for a diagnosis or a prescription treatment plan. If your dog is limping, painful, or struggling to move around, they need a proper veterinary evaluation first. Boswellia may then become part of that plan, but it should not stand in for it.

What Boswellia Is Not

It is worth being honest about the limits. Boswellia is not a miracle. It does not rebuild damaged cartilage overnight, and it is not a substitute for prescription pain medication in dogs with severe osteoarthritis.

It is also worth remembering that supplements in general receive less regulatory scrutiny than pharmaceuticals. The FDA does not review non-drug supplements for safety or effectiveness before they hit shelves, which is why quality markers and veterinary guidance matter.

What boswellia can be — with the right product, the right dog, and reasonable expectations — is a genuinely useful part of a joint care plan. That is a smaller claim than the marketing sometimes makes, and a bigger deal than most single herbal supplements can back up with actual research.

The Bigger Picture on Aging Joints

Boswellia works best as part of a broader strategy rather than a stand-alone fix. Dogs with aging joints tend to do best with a combination of approaches: weight management, moderate consistent exercise, comfortable orthopedic bedding, and, when appropriate, targeted supplements and veterinary-directed care.

If your dog is at the stage where you are starting to notice the slower mornings and the extra sighs when they settle down, that is the moment to have a conversation with your veterinarian. There is a lot that can be done to keep an aging body comfortable, and boswellia may earn a spot in that plan.

A supplement pulled from a tree resin used for thousands of years is a nice reminder that helpful ideas sometimes have very long roots. Combined with modern research, thoughtful formulation, and a good veterinarian, it becomes one more tool in the effort to give a beloved dog many more comfortable, mobile years.

Sources and References

  • 1,3,5,13,14,16,19 BioPup, November 24, 2025
  • 2,7,18 Chewy, June 16, 2026
  • 4 Journal of Psychiatric Research, October 2026 Pages 381-390, Volume 201
  • 6 Schweiz Arch Tierheilkd. 2004 Feb;146(2):71-9
  • 8 PLoS One. 2022 Feb 16;17(2):e0263971
  • 9 Nat Prod Res. 2023 Jun;37(11):1782-1786
  • 10,12 PLoS One. 2024 Oct 30;19(10):e0305697
  • 11 Animals 2023, 13(5), 870
  • 15,17 VCA Hospitals, Boswellia

Just because something is natural does not mean it plays nicely with every other medication. Boswellia should not be given alongside drugs that affect blood clotting or platelet function, including aspirin, heparin, warfarin, and other blood thinners.

It should also be used with caution, or avoided entirely, in pregnant or nursing dogs, since safe use has not been established in those situations. Always share a full list of your dog's medications and supplements with your veterinarian before starting anything new.15,16

How to Give It

Boswellia comes in several forms: powders, capsules, and tablets. It can be given with or without food, ideally at the same time each day. Remember these practical guidelines:17,18,19

  • Use a dog-specific product — Human boswellia supplements may contain ingredients, combinations, or dosages that are not appropriate for dogs. When possible, choose a supplement made specifically for pets.
  • Look for standardization — Products standardized for AKBA content tend to deliver more consistent results. Advanced extracts with improved bioavailability can achieve stronger effects at lower doses.
  • Check for quality markers — Supplements produced in National Animal Supplement Council (NASC) certified facilities that follow Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) generally offer better assurance of ingredient purity and label accuracy.
  • Be patient with the timeline — Most dogs show improvement within two to four weeks of consistent use, though some may take up to eight weeks to show significant changes. This is a supplement that rewards patience, not one that produces overnight results.
  • And loop in your veterinarian — Boswellia is not a replacement for a diagnosis or a prescription treatment plan. If your dog is limping, painful, or struggling to move around, they need a proper veterinary evaluation first. Boswellia may then become part of that plan, but it should not stand in for it.

What Boswellia Is Not

It is worth being honest about the limits. Boswellia is not a miracle. It does not rebuild damaged cartilage overnight, and it is not a substitute for prescription pain medication in dogs with severe osteoarthritis.

It is also worth remembering that supplements in general receive less regulatory scrutiny than pharmaceuticals. The FDA does not review non-drug supplements for safety or effectiveness before they hit shelves, which is why quality markers and veterinary guidance matter.

What boswellia can be — with the right product, the right dog, and reasonable expectations — is a genuinely useful part of a joint care plan. That is a smaller claim than the marketing sometimes makes, and a bigger deal than most single herbal supplements can back up with actual research.

The Bigger Picture on Aging Joints

Boswellia works best as part of a broader strategy rather than a stand-alone fix. Dogs with aging joints tend to do best with a combination of approaches: weight management, moderate consistent exercise, comfortable orthopedic bedding, and, when appropriate, targeted supplements and veterinary-directed care.

If your dog is at the stage where you are starting to notice the slower mornings and the extra sighs when they settle down, that is the moment to have a conversation with your veterinarian. There is a lot that can be done to keep an aging body comfortable, and boswellia may earn a spot in that plan.

A supplement pulled from a tree resin used for thousands of years is a nice reminder that helpful ideas sometimes have very long roots. Combined with modern research, thoughtful formulation, and a good veterinarian, it becomes one more tool in the effort to give a beloved dog many more comfortable, mobile years.
